description: O projeto consiste no desenvolvimento de uma aplicação web interativa que consome dados de observação da Terra da NASA (humidade do solo, precipitação histórica e temperatura da superfície) para criar um sistema preditivo voltado ao setor agrícola moçambicano.
summary: MozAgro Global AI transforms free NASA data into simple, plain-language answers for farmers, addressing the core question: “Can I plant now?” Users can select a specific point on a map (ranging from 1 m² to 3 km²) or choose an entire district in Mozambique from the available options. The system provides guidance on the best crops for both the rainy and dry seasons, estimates the number of days until harvest, and identifies the optimal months for planting. It also issues alerts regarding local risks—such as drought, floods, high winds, cyclones, soil erosion, extreme heat, frost, pests, and diseases—while assessing soil degradation and suggesting recovery measures. Additionally, the tool offers an analysis of land use, a 30-day climate outlook, and a downloadable PDF report. Built using NASA POWER, MODIS, and NASA GIBS, the platform currently functions as a heuristic prototype that has not yet been calibrated by agronomists.

MozAgro Global AI — Detailed Description (for the NASA Space Apps form)

Paste the Full version into "Detailed Description". If the form has a character limit, use the Short version at the end. Replace the items in [BRACKETS] before submitting (team facts, and the statement about what was verified live). Delete this note.

FULL VERSION

1. The problem

Smallholder farmers in Mozambique, and in many regions of the world, decide when and what to plant with little technical information. Rains are erratic, droughts, floods and cyclones are frequent, and soils wear out. NASA publishes free Earth-observation data that could help, but it comes in technical formats (NetCDF, HDF, index values such as NDVI) that farmers and extension workers cannot easily read.

2. What MozAgro Global AI does

MozAgro Global AI is a web platform that turns NASA data into a decision written in everyday language. The user clicks anywhere on the map and chooses a zone from 1 m² (a garden bed) to 3 km² (a large field). In Mozambique the user can also analyse a whole municipality or district (no 3 km² limit) and print a dedicated PDF report. The main question answered is: "Can I plant now?", shown as a traffic light:

  • 🟢 Green: good time to plant.
  • 🟡 Yellow: it is possible, but care or investment (for example irrigation) is needed. A dry place is not "forbidden": it only means water must be supplied.
  • 🔴 Red: reserved for places that are definitely bad for farming (open water, ice, built-up areas, desert, extreme cold).

For each analysed place the platform provides:

  1. Crops by season. For the rainy and the dry season, crops ranked from most to least suitable, chosen from the crops most commonly grown in the user's continental region (Southern, Eastern, Western/Central and Northern Africa, Europe, Asia, North America, Latin America, Oceania). The catalogue has 29 crops and crop groups (for example maize, cowpea, cassava, rice, sorghum, millet, sweet potato, groundnut, vegetables, tomato and onion, cotton, cashew, banana, sugarcane, coffee and cocoa, wheat, potato, soy, olive, vine, citrus, apple and pear).
  2. Time to harvest and best months to plant. For each crop, the estimated days from planting to harvest (adjusted to the local temperature with growing-degree-days; trees show years to first harvest) and the best sowing months, found by testing every possible sowing month against the local monthly temperature, rainfall and soil moisture. The expected harvest month is shown too.
  3. Daily irrigation advice. When a crop needs extra water, the platform says how much: litres per m² per day, litres per day for the whole analysed area, and the equivalent in 10-litre buckets, with the intensity (little, moderate, much irrigation). It is the cycle's water deficit spread over the crop-cycle days, so it is an average (on hot dry days more is needed, on rainy days less).
  4. Risks of the region ("Risks and soil" tab). Empirical probabilities from about 25 years of NASA POWER daily data: drought (share of years with a dry rainy season and with 14+ consecutive dry days), floods and waterlogging (days with 50 mm or 100 mm of rain, days of saturated soil), strong wind and cyclones (days above 62 km/h and 39 km/h), soil erosion (modified Fournier rainfall-erosivity index combined with NDVI cover and relief), extreme heat and frost, and pests and diseases (climate favourability for fungi, caterpillars such as fall armyworm, and whitefly; it is a climate indicator, not an observation of pests). Each risk lists the reasons in plain words, what to do, and how it was computed. A per-crop table shows which risks matter most for the region's most suitable crops. Earthquakes are explicitly not estimated, because the NASA data used do not measure seismic hazard.
  5. Soil health from the point of view of wear. An indicator of the pressure on the soil (erosion, fast loss of organic matter in hot climates, low vegetation cover, frequent droughts, current soil moisture, continuous cultivation) turned into a "soil health" level (good / fair / fragile), the three main causes, and concrete recovery and improvement actions (organic matter, legume rotation, cover crops, contour lines and vegetative barriers, mulching, water-harvesting pits, agroforestry, and a laboratory soil test). NASA does not measure pH, nutrients, organic matter or texture, so the platform says so and recommends a soil analysis.
  6. Relief. Plain, plateau or mountain, from the elevation returned by NASA POWER, with its effect on farming (cooler nights, frost, erosion on slopes).
  7. Trees and scrub. From MODIS land cover, it tells whether the land is practically free ("good for planting"), has scrub to clear, or is forest where trees would have to be cut, with a warning about permits and the dangers of uncontrolled burning.
  8. Land occupation hint. Water, built-up, partly occupied, cultivated or free land, with an explicit low confidence: isolated houses and small roads are not visible at 500 m, and ownership cannot be seen from space (in Mozambique land use rights are DUAT and land is not sold).
  9. Next 30 days. A climate-based outlook (long-term normal plus evapotranspiration balance in four blocks, farming phase of the season, crops of the month and cyclone-season notices). It is not a weather forecast and says so.
  10. Plain-language interpretation of every number. NDVI, EVI and SAVI are explained in words ("sparse vegetation: dry grass or crops just emerging"), rainfall is described as "it rains little / a lot" instead of millimetres, and technical details are moved to the "NASA data" tab and to the PDF report, so that the main screen stays simple.

3. How NASA data makes it possible

All inputs to the analysis are NASA data:

  • NASA POWER (MERRA-2-based): monthly climatology (temperature, precipitation, humidity, solar radiation); daily series (precipitation, temperature, humidity, root-zone and surface soil wetness GWETROOT/GWETTOP/GWETPROF) for the "plant now?" decision; a daily history since 2001 (precipitation, maximum and minimum temperature, 10 m wind, soil wetness) for the risk probabilities; and the elevation of the grid cell for the relief class.
  • MODIS Terra MOD13Q1 (through the ORNL DAAC MODIS web service): NDVI, EVI, pixel reliability and red/NIR reflectance, from which SAVI = 1.5·(NIR−Red)/(NIR+Red+0.5) is computed.
  • MODIS MCD12Q1 (through the ORNL DAAC): IGBP land cover used for land type, tree/scrub cover and occupation.
  • NASA GIBS: satellite imagery for the map background.

Administrative boundaries (geoBoundaries) are only used to draw and select districts on the map; they are not part of the analysis.

4. How it works (method)

A transparent, rule-based engine, not a black box. For each crop, trapezoid suitability functions score temperature, water, soil moisture, calendar and vegetation, combined with a "law of the minimum" so one limiting factor cannot be hidden by the average. The rainy season is detected as the six consecutive wettest months at the clicked location, so it works in both hemispheres. "Can I plant now?" uses the last 7 days of root-zone soil wetness and the last 30 days of rain, with the temperature and the land cover as safety checks. Risks are empirical frequencies over about 25 years, combined into 0–100 scores with the formulas shown to the user. Area limits (1 m² to 3 km²) are validated in the browser and again on the server. The backend is written in Python (FastAPI) without compiled dependencies, uses a SQLite cache, runs all external calls off the event loop, and degrades gracefully: only the climate data is mandatory; if a satellite source is unavailable the app says so, explains the technical reason and continues with the rest.

5. User experience

Login for the demonstration needs only a name. The user picks a place on the map or in a list, chooses the zone size, and presses "Analyse". The result opens with the traffic light and the reasons in plain words, followed by cards, alerts and tabs: What to plant, Risks and soil, NASA data, History and How it works. A printable PDF report gives all the technical detail (crop cycles, ideal temperature and water, daily irrigation, risks, soil recovery actions). The interface works on a phone and keeps working if the map layer fails.

6. Impact, relevance and creativity

  • Impact: it lowers the barrier between NASA data and planting decisions for people with little technical background, with a focus on Mozambique (climate-vulnerable and cyclone-prone) and the ability to work anywhere on Earth.
  • Relevance: the questions answered (when to plant, what to plant, how much to irrigate, what could go wrong, how to protect and recover the soil) are the ones farmers and extension services actually ask.
  • Creativity: one click turns several NASA datasets into a single plain-language decision, with a traffic light that distinguishes "needs investment" from "do not plant", district-level analysis with a printable report, and explicit honesty about what satellites cannot see.

7. Validity, limitations and honesty

  • The decision engine, crop parameters, thresholds and soil/pest indicators are heuristics from general agronomic references, not calibrated with local agronomists or field measurements. Crop cycles, growing-degree-days and pest-favourable climate windows are general agronomic references, not NASA data, and are labelled as such in the app.
  • NASA POWER cells are about 50 km and MODIS pixels 250–500 m, so values for a small plot describe the surrounding region. Elevation is a grid-cell average: it cannot see hills, slopes or valleys inside the cell.
  • MODIS land cover cannot show isolated houses, small roads or land ownership.
  • The 30-day outlook is a climatological expectation, not a forecast. Pest risk is climate favourability, not a pest observation. The wind and cyclone risk is a statistical indicator and the 50 km grid smooths real gusts. Earthquakes are not estimated.
  • NASA does not measure soil pH, organic matter, nutrients or texture, so the soil-health result is a pressure-of-wear indicator and the app recommends a laboratory soil test.
  • SMAP, GPM, GRACE/GRACE-FO, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, SRTM and the Prithvi foundation model are not integrated (they require Earthdata login, raster tooling or model weights). Soil moisture, precipitation and elevation come from NASA POWER/MERRA-2, not from those missions.
  • The interface is in Portuguese (the language of the target users); the demo, documentation and this form are in English. [EDIT if an English interface is added.]
  • [EDIT/CONFIRM: state truthfully which data sources were verified working on the live app at submission time. If the MODIS vegetation or land-cover calls were not working, say so here and remove the claims that depend on them.]
  • The code logic is covered by automated tests that use simulated API responses (32 tests).

8. Use of artificial intelligence

AI tools (Claude by Anthropic and Gemini by Google) were used to write and review code (backend, frontend, tests), documentation and drafts of these texts. Every AI-assisted code file has an "AI DISCLOSURE" header; the app shows an AI disclosure in "How it works" and in the PDF report. AI did not generate the photographs (real, credited photos) and AI-written code does not fabricate data: all figures shown come from NASA services or from documented formulas applied to them. [CONFIRM: the idea, scope, choice of data sources and decision rules were defined by the team; AI assisted with implementation and review. Keep this sentence only if true.]

9. Future work

Calibration of thresholds with agronomists at five pilot sites (Beira, Chimoio, Nampula, Maputo, Lichinga); official district boundaries (INE/CENACARTA); a Portuguese/English interface switch; SMAP and GPM integration through Earthdata login and per-district pre-computed tables; a separate notebook using HLS imagery and Prithvi-EO for built-up masks; and field validation with extension services.
